title: State EOC Duty Officer — Checkpoint Staffing and Guard Timeline

fields.systemName: Recorded Line - EOC Director Desk, Training Room

caller.name: State EOC Duty Officer
caller.label: Minnesota State Emergency Operations Center, St. Paul

callee.name: Marcus Lindqvist
callee.label: County Emergency Management Director (Sheriff Dale Rademacher conferenced in, 555-0120)

transcript.speaker: State EOC Duty Officer
transcript.text: Director, this is the state EOC duty officer in St. Paul. We've seen your staffing note. Is the Sheriff on the line?

transcript.speaker: State EOC Duty Officer
transcript.text: Good. Let me read back what you sent. Eleven checkpoint sites, two people per site, around the clock. That's twenty-two per shift, and sixty-six across three eight-hour shifts. Correct me if I'm wrong.

transcript.speaker: State EOC Duty Officer
transcript.text: Against that, you have four deputies free for checkpoints today. Pell County gives you two from eleven-thirty to about nineteen-thirty. Ritter, nothing until tomorrow's day shift. So tonight you're looking at eleven sites and maybe four people.

transcript.speaker: State EOC Duty Officer
transcript.text: If you want National Guard soldiers on checkpoints, the Governor's office normally wants a county emergency declaration from your Board of Commissioners on file with the request. The request comes through us here at the state EOC, through Homeland Security and Emergency Management.

transcript.speaker: State EOC Duty Officer
transcript.text: Timing. If the request and the declaration reach us by noon, the earliest arrival is about eighteen hundred tonight. Without them, it's tomorrow afternoon at best. That's not a decision I can make for you. I just need to know what's coming so I can tee it up.

transcript.speaker: State EOC Duty Officer
transcript.text: And Sheriff, while you work it, I'd recommend you send us a site-by-site list. Which of the eleven are staffed, which ones carry the turkey, feed, shavings and rendering traffic, and which ones could go dark tonight. Guard planners will ask for that first.

transcript.speaker: State EOC Duty Officer
transcript.text: So, Director. Are you going to your Board, and when can I expect a request, or a call telling me there won't be one?

transcript.speaker: Text message to Director Marcus Lindqvist from the County Board Chair, 10:16
transcript.text: Do we need to meet at 11:00 to declare? If we do, Northland 9 and the Ledger will be in the room and they'll ask the farm name.

voiceStyles.State EOC Duty Officer: Calm, businesslike state duty officer in his 50s, reads numbers slowly and precisely, phones ringing faintly behind him
voiceStyles.Sheriff Rademacher: Gruff rural sheriff in his 60s, brief, on a cell phone in a patrol car
voiceStyles.Text message to Director Marcus Lindqvis: Read flatly by the facilitator as a text message

instructorNote: This is a decision point. The Director has until about 11:30 to decide whether to ask the Commissioners for a county emergency declaration and send a National Guard checkpoint request through the state EOC. Watch for three things: the Sheriff should produce a site-by-site coverage plan that staffs the turkey, feed, shavings and rendering roads first and flags any site that could go unmanned for more than 2 hours, which triggers escalation. Nobody should set up county-only roadblocks. The PIO should be told what the declaration will say and that it will not name the farm.
